frameworks.name: Directive Specificity as Talent Indicator
frameworks.definition: A framework for evaluating an employee's capability level by observing the level of specificity required in job directives, from high-level objectives (executive) to granular instructions (individual contributor).

frameworks.name: Talent Tier Progression
frameworks.definition: A salary-based framework showing how each incremental hire reveals a new level of capability, with the gap between tiers representing a distinct quality jump.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi observes that as entrepreneurs scale, the level of talent they can attract increases dramatically while their tolerance for mediocrity decreases. At each salary tier (from $50k to $1M+), recognizable jumps in capability occur—a $50k employee reveals what good talent looks like, then $75k shows the gap, $100k is a new caliber, and so on, with each tier representing a night-and-day difference in intelligence, work ethic, and experience.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi: Senior hires ($1M+) bring entire teams with them—typically two to four people from previous companies they've worked with. This allows them to arrive with fully built organizational infrastructure: they know the systems, have pre-selected talent, possess operational playbooks, and can stand up entire functions (e.g., finance or acquisition) immediately without requiring direction.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Senior talent brings proven networks and systems that eliminate ramp-up time and reduce management overhead.

numbers.axis: Compensation level (USD) and team size brought

claims.text: Alex Hormozi: The level of specificity required in directives is the primary signal of a person's capability. A true executive needs only high-level objectives ('build out acquisition for this business'); a mid-level leader requires specific campaign directives; a manager needs tactical guidance (specific angles, copy hooks); an individual contributor needs granular instruction (reading level, tone).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Fewer and higher-level directives indicate greater capability to autonomously set priorities and execute with minimal input.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi: A person is not ready for promotion if the manager must still perform work that should be delegated to them. For example, if a manager must conduct tough conversations with a leader's team on the leader's behalf, that person lacks leadership capability and is not ready for advancement.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Leadership requires the ability to make hard decisions and have difficult conversations independently; if the boss must do this, it reveals a gap.
bounded_by: Does not apply to individual contributors

claims.text: Alex Hormozi: If hired as a C-suite executive to run an entire function, the person should not be given detailed directives on how to execute. They should bring domain expertise, strategic thinking, and improvements the hiring manager does not anticipate. Needing to reprioritize their schedule or issue step-by-step directives means they are a director at best, not C-suite.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: C-suite talent is valued precisely because they require minimal direction and bring knowledge gaps to the organization; excessive direction indicates misclassification.
bounded_by: Does not apply to middle management or junior hires

claims.text: Alex Hormozi: Gym Launch's team quality differed significantly from Acquisition.com's current team. Approximately six to seven Acquisition.com employees earn over $1M annually, representing a vastly higher caliber of talent in the same founder's operation at a later scaling stage.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Same founder, different businesses at different scales

examples.text: When Alex Hormozi hired his first $50,000-per-year employee at Gym Launch, he was struck by how much better this person was than prior hires and thought 'holy shit, this is what talent looks like.' When he hired his first $75,000 employee, the difference was even more stark—he realized $50k was not good enough. This progression continued with each tier, including his first six-figure employee (where he initially expected someone exceptional enough to 'cure cancer'), then $250k, $500k, $1M, and beyond, each representing night-and-day improvements in intelligence, work ethic, and experience.

If asked to build an entire acquisition function from scratch, Alex Hormozi would not go alone. He would instead bring six people he has already worked with from prior companies, because he already knows their capabilities, has established relationships, and understands the infrastructure needed. He would arrive with pre-selected controllers, known financial systems, and pre-built playbooks, allowing him to stand up the entire function immediately.

practices.text: When evaluating a person's readiness for promotion, assess whether you still perform work that should be delegated to them—such as conducting tough conversations with their team. If you are, they are not yet a leader.
When hiring a C-suite executive, give high-level directives only (e.g., 'build out acquisition'). If you find yourself giving specific tactical directions, the hire is not C-level caliber.
Prioritize hiring for grit and capability over immediate technical skills. At higher levels, talent brings entire teams and established systems that eliminate ramp-up time.
